A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LessonL study and provide readable main text, tables, figures, algorithms, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, including the Geometry and DFT case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-optimization experiments, LessonL code-generation results, component ablations, and case studies. These qualify independently of the GPT code-generation scores attributed to the EvalPlus leaderboard.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds reasoning-model comparisons, agent-count and longer-round experiments, and additional collaboration and failure analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C retain the same lesson solicitation, banking, selection, effectiveness adjustment, and solution-selection procedures. Appendix G.3 rewords the code-generation exception concerning SELECTHIGHSPEEDUP, but Section 3.4 retains selection by passed-test counts and relevance; no changed procedure is established.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ParEval and PolyBench in serial/OpenMP modes and HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, and MBPP+ for code generation. The added case studies concern existing ParEval tasks. SWE-bench is mentioned as future coverage, not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 adds DeepseekR1-14B and OpenAI o3 to the code-optimization and cost comparisons, introducing a substantial new category of reasoning-model comparators. Existing baselines remain, and the comparator membership in the code-generation comparison, Table 2, is unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments evaluate teams of three through six agents against a one-agent reference and extend the round-budget analysis to ten rounds. Appendix I adds per-problem LLM-call and token-accounting metrics. The primary evaluation procedures, performance metrics, and default hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and iteration analysis, v2 adds agent-count sensitivity, a longer-round study, comparisons against the best constituent agent, and a lesson-transfer example for sorting complex numbers. Appendix M adds a dedicated LessonL failure case. These substantially expand analysis of scaling, complementarity, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Tables 1 and 3 continue reporting means and standard deviations over three runs, including the added reasoning-model rows. Seed matching and runtime-benchmarking procedures are retained. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test, or repeated-run disclosure is introduced.

E6.justification: Previously reported scores are retained, but new comparator results change rankings: Table 1 adds OpenAI o3 at 2.21 ± 0.16 speedup on serial ParEval, versus LessonL's unchanged 2.16 ± 0.11. Tables 4 and 9–11 add agent-count, resource-consumption, category-level, and ten-round results. New case studies report successful lesson transfer and optimization failures.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and reasoning, including the effectiveness adjustment and DFT Equation (1), are retained. The DFT appendix is renumbered from K to L. No new formal assumption, theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about lesson-based collaboration, complementary agent strengths, competitive coding performance, and small-model teams outperforming a larger model under similar resource budgets. Updated case-study references do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 qualifies comparative superiority in light of OpenAI o3. v2 adds interpretations of diminishing returns from more agents and rounds, explicitly acknowledges function-level rather than repository-level applicability, and motivates external knowledge as a possible response to failures. Appendix J attributes category-level regressions to generation randomness.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an implementation repository URL on the first page and in new Appendix N. It also identifies the additional models and documents their pricing and assumed model configurations for cost estimation. Existing prompt templates, benchmark adaptations, hardware descriptions, and default hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Agent Hospital and DEI to the related-work discussion. References are also added for the new models and SWE-bench. The positioning of LessonL around exchanging lessons, relative to role-based collaboration and solution aggregation, remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language edits, labels the existing algorithm sketch, expands experimental and limitations discussions, and adds appendices J, M, and N. Existing case studies are renumbered, the contents listing becomes appendix-focused, and affiliation, conference, and funding information is updated. The main narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4 and 9–11, expands benchmark and cost tables, and redraws Figure 4 with reasoning-model points and an updated Pareto front. Several displays are relocated or resized, the algorithm sketch is boxed, and Table 3 gains result highlighting. These are localized additions and formatting changes within the retained visual design.

improvement.justification: The reasoning-model comparisons, collaboration/scaling analyses, explicit failure case, and code-access disclosure make v2 more informative and better qualified than v1. The gain is limited by unresolved reporting inconsistencies: new Table 9 reports 20,453 MoA tokens per problem, whereas Table 7's totals over 60 problems imply about 10,429. Overall, the stronger comparative evidence and clearer applicability limits outweigh this localized accounting problem.
